stem:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Examination shows deep, rapid breathing and a fruity odor on the breath. Laboratory studies reveal hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and a low serum bicarbonate.

Immune destruction of which of the following cell types most directly explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.misconception: Loss of the glucose-raising hormone is being treated as the cause of ketoacidosis.
options.explanation: Alpha-cell loss would reduce glucagon, which would not produce insulin-deficient ketoacidosis; the autoimmune target in type 1 diabetes is the beta cell.

options.label: B
options.misconception: An inhibitory islet cell is being treated as the primary autoimmune target.
options.explanation: Delta cells secrete somatostatin; type 1 diabetes is driven by immune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells, not delta cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes
options.misconception: Exocrine pancreatic injury is being confused with endocrine insulin deficiency.
options.explanation: Acinar destruction causes exocrine insufficiency, not the absolute insulin deficiency that drives ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes.

options.label: D
options.misconception: None; autoimmune beta-cell loss causes absolute insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes develops when the immune system destroys pancreatic beta cells that make insulin; without insulin, cells use fat for fuel and produce acidic ketones, yielding ketoacidosis.

options.label: E
options.text: PP cells that secrete pancreatic polypeptide
options.misconception: A minor islet cell type is being treated as the source of insulin deficiency.
options.explanation: PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide; they are not the cells whose destruction produces absolute insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.

context: Learning objective: link type 1 autoimmune beta-cell loss to ketoacidosis. Without insulin, tissues rely on fat; ketone production acidifies the blood. Deep rapid breathing and fruity acetone breath are early clinical signs of diabetic ketoacidosis.
